questions.stem:
A chemical solution is said to be an acid if its pH level is less than 7, a base if its pH level is greater than 7, and neutral otherwise.
Figure 1 displays a flowchart of an algorithm that, for a given pH entered by the user, displays whether it is an acid, a base or neutral.
questions.fig: Figure 1: flowchart Start → INPUT pH → decision A (TRUE → OUTPUT “Acid”; arrow B down) → decision pH > 7 (arrow C across → output D; FALSE down) → output E → Stop.

parts.q: Complete the table below to indicate the text that should appear in the flowchart for the letters A-E.
parts.ask: Fill in the missing text for the boxes and arrows A to E.
parts.scheme: A: pH < 7; B: FALSE; C: TRUE; D: OUTPUT “Base”; E: OUTPUT “Neutral”. Each correct response 1 mark.
parts.model: A: pH < 7, B: FALSE, C: TRUE, D: OUTPUT "Base", E: OUTPUT "Neutral"

idea.title: Flowchart shapes
idea.text: A diamond is a decision, with a TRUE arrow and a FALSE arrow leaving it. A parallelogram is an input or an output. A rounded box is Start or Stop.

steps.say: A is the first decision, and its TRUE arrow outputs "Acid", so A must test for an acid: pH < 7.
B is the other arrow out of diamond A, so it is the FALSE branch.
C leaves the pH > 7 diamond sideways; the downward arrow is labelled FALSE, so C is TRUE.
pH > 7 being TRUE means a base, so D outputs "Base".
Reaching E means pH is neither less than nor greater than 7, so it is 7: E outputs "Neutral".

parts.tip: Copy the style of the given box: write OUTPUT "Base", not just Base.

questions.stem:
You have eight coins and a two pan scales. Both the coins and the scales are gold plated and the diameter and circumference of all the coins are exactly the same. The coins are worth €2 each, a total of €16.
- seven of the coins are genuine and weigh the same amount.
- one of the coins is fake and is heavier than the others.

parts.q: Explain a way that the fake coin can be found in the minimum number of weighings.
parts.ask: Explain how to find the heavy coin in as few weighings as possible.

points.text: Weighing 1: place a group of 3 coins on each pan
If they weigh the same, the fake is among the other 2: place each of those on the pans (weighing 2)
If not, weigh 2 of the 3 coins from the heavier side: if they balance the 3rd coin is fake, otherwise the heavier one is (weighing 2)

parts.scheme: The minimum is 2 weighings: place 3 coins on each pan (weighing 1). If they weigh the same, the fake is among the other 2, found by placing each of them on the pans (weighing 2). If they don't weigh the same, choose 2 of the 3 coins on the heavier side and weigh them (weighing 2): if they are the same, the 3rd coin is the fake; if not, the heavier coin is. Valid solution with 2 weighings 3 marks; valid solution with 3 or more weighings 2 marks; reasonable attempt 1 mark.
parts.model: Put 3 coins on each pan and keep 2 aside (weighing 1). If the pans balance, the fake is one of the 2 kept aside, so weigh them against each other and the heavier one is fake (weighing 2). If one pan is heavier, weigh 2 of its 3 coins against each other (weighing 2): if they balance the third coin is fake, otherwise the heavier one is.

idea.title: Each weighing has three outcomes
idea.text: A two-pan scale can tip left, tip right or balance, so one weighing can split the coins into three groups. 8 coins become groups of 3, 3 and 2; at most 3 coins are left, and one more weighing finds the fake among them.

steps.say: Split the 8 coins into three groups, 3, 3 and 2, because a weighing has three possible results.
Weighing 1: 3 against 3. If they balance, the fake is in the 2 left out; if not, it is in the heavier 3.
Weighing 2, if they balanced: weigh the 2 left-out coins against each other; the heavier is fake.
Weighing 2, if they didn't: weigh 2 of the heavier 3. A tip shows the fake; a balance means it is the third coin.

parts.tip: Halving (4 v 4, then 2 v 2, then 1 v 1) needs 3 weighings and earns only 2 marks.

parts.q: Outline briefly your use of abstraction to tackle this problem.
parts.ask: Say how you used abstraction to solve the coin problem.

points.text: By ignoring irrelevant details such as coin colour, size and value

parts.scheme: By ignoring irrelevant details such as coin colour, size and value. Very good description 2 marks.
parts.model: I used abstraction by ignoring the details that make no difference, such as the gold plating, the coins' diameter and circumference and their €2 value, and focusing only on what matters: the weight of each coin.

idea.title: Abstraction
idea.text: Abstraction means removing the details that don't affect a problem, so you can focus on the ones that do.

steps.say: List the details you are given: gold plating, diameter, circumference, €2 value and weight.
Only the weight helps to find the fake; the rest is irrelevant and is ignored. That is abstraction.

parts.tip: Name the actual details you ignored, taken from the question.

questions.stem:
The reproduction rules for honey bees are quite remarkable. Females lay eggs and if an egg is fertilised by a male it will hatch as a female. Unfertilised eggs hatch as males.
The illustration below shows an ancestry tree for the male honey bee shown at the top of the tree. There are five generations shown.
questions.fig: Photo of honey bees; an ancestry tree (M = male bee, they only have a mother; F = female bee, they have a mother and a father): Generation 1 M; 2 F; 3 F, M; 4 F, M, F; 5 F, M, F, M, F; empty space below for more generations.

parts.q: Draw and label two additional generations.
parts.ask: Draw and label generations 6 and 7 of the bee ancestry tree.
parts.scheme: Full correct response 3 marks; one fully correct generation 2 marks; two or more branches from generation 7 fully complete 2 marks; any correct value 1 mark. Generation 6: F M | F | F M | F | F M (8 bees). Generation 7: F M F | F M | F M F | F M | F M F (13 bees).
parts.model: Generation 6 (8 bees): each F in generation 5 gets a mother and a father (F and M) and each M gets only a mother (F): F M, F, F M, F, F M. Generation 7 (13 bees): F M, F, F M, F M, F, F M, F M, F.

idea.title: Parents by rule
idea.text: A male has only a mother: one parent, F. A female has a mother and a father: two parents, F and M. Apply this rule to every bee in the bottom row to grow the next generation.

steps.say: Go along generation 5 (F, M, F, M, F) and draw each bee's parents below it, joined to it by lines.
Each F gets two parents, F and M; each M gets one, F. Generation 6: F M | F | F M | F | F M, 8 bees.
Do the same to generation 6 to get generation 7: 13 bees, 8 females and 5 males.
Check by counting each generation: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

parts.tip: Label the new rows 'Generation 6' and 'Generation 7' and join each bee to its child with a line.

parts.q: Describe any pattern emerging that could be used to model the number of bees in any particular generation.
parts.ask: Describe the pattern in the number of bees in each generation.

points.text: The number of bees in each generation is the sum of the number of bees in the previous two generations (Fibonacci sequence)

parts.scheme: The number of bees at each generation is the sum of the number of bees at the previous two generations (Fibonacci sequence). Very good description 2 marks; fair description 1 mark.
parts.model: The number of bees in each generation is the sum of the numbers in the two generations before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … This is the Fibonacci sequence.

idea.title: Fibonacci
idea.text: In the Fibonacci sequence each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … For the bees it works because every bee has a mother (all of the previous generation) and only females also have a father.

steps.say: Count the bees in each generation, including your two new ones.
See how each number is made from the two before it.
State the rule: each generation is the sum of the previous two generations (the Fibonacci sequence).

parts.tip: Give the rule in words, not just the name 'Fibonacci'.

questions.stem:
The state transition diagram for a particular Turing machine is shown in Figure 3 below.
The initial state is S0 and the initial tape contents is the binary number 0110 followed by a blank, represented by ‘B’. The final state is S3.
questions.fig: Figure 3: state diagram, each arrow labelled (symbol read, symbol written): S0 → S1 (1,0); S0 → S2 (0,0); S1 loops (1,1); S1 → S2 (0,1); S2 → S1 (1,0); S2 loops (0,0); S1 → S3 (B,B); S2 → S3 (B,B). Beside it a trace: state S0 with tape 0 1 1 0 B (head under the first 0), then five rows of an empty state box and tape cells.

parts.q: Trace the computation of the Turing machine by filling in the blanks in the diagram below. The read/write head is currently reading a 0. You can assume that the read/write head is moved one place to the right at the end of each step.
parts.ask: Fill in the state and the tape after each of the five steps.
parts.scheme: States S2, S1, S1, S2, S3 with tapes 0110B, 0010B, 0010B, 0011B, 0011B (the head one cell further right each time). Full correct response 5 marks; three or more correct tapes 3 marks; two correct tapes 2 marks; one correct tape 1 mark.

idea.title: Reading a transition
idea.text: Each arrow is labelled (read, write). In the current state, find the arrow whose first symbol matches the cell under the head, write its second symbol into that cell, follow the arrow to the new state, then move the head one cell to the right.

steps.say: Step 1: in S0 the head reads 0. Arrow (0,0) leads to S2: write 0 (no change) and move right.
Step 2: in S2 the head reads 1. Arrow (1,0) leads to S1: the 1 becomes 0.
Step 3: in S1 the head reads 1. The loop (1,1) writes 1 and stays in S1.
Step 4: in S1 the head reads 0. Arrow (0,1) leads to S2: the 0 becomes 1.
Step 5: in S2 the head reads B. Arrow (B,B) leads to S3, the final state. The tape stays 0011B.

parts.tip: Write out the whole tape after every step, even when nothing changes: each correct tape earns marks.

parts.q:
A simplified version of the selection sort algorithm involves the use of two lists called list1 and list2. At the start of the algorithm the elements in list1 are unsorted, and list2 is empty as shown.

At the end of the algorithm list1 is empty, and list2 contains the elements that were in list1 at the start, now sorted in ascending order.

The algorithm is described by the following pseudo-code:
```
1. Let N be the number of elements in list1
2. Initialise an empty list of length N – call this list2
3. Repeat N times:
4.      Select the smallest (minimum) element from list1
5.      Move the smallest element from list1 to list2
6. Stop
```

Apply the algorithm to sort the list of integers [15, 28, 14, 21] showing the state of both lists after each pass of the algorithm. Pass #1 has been completed for you. You only need to fill in the numbers for passes 2, 3 and 4.
parts.ask: Show what is in list1 and list2 after passes 2, 3 and 4.
parts.scheme: Each correct pass 1 mark. Pass #2: list1 _, 28, _, 21 and list2 14, 15. Pass #3: list1 _, 28, _, _ and list2 14, 15, 21. Pass #4: list1 empty and list2 14, 15, 21, 28.
parts.model: Pass #2: list1 = 28, 21 and list2 = 14, 15. Pass #3: list1 = 28 and list2 = 14, 15, 21. Pass #4: list1 is empty and list2 = 14, 15, 21, 28.

idea.title: Selection sort
idea.text: Each pass selects the smallest value that is still unsorted and puts it in the next place of the sorted list, so after pass k the k smallest values are in order.

steps.say: Pass 2: the smallest value left in list1 (15, 28, 21) is 15. Move it to list2: list2 = 14, 15.
Pass 3: the smallest of 28 and 21 is 21. Move it: list2 = 14, 15, 21; only 28 is left in list1.
Pass 4: move the last value, 28. list1 is empty and list2 = 14, 15, 21, 28.

parts.q: The algorithm sorts the list in ascending order. What changes would you need to make to the algorithm so that it sorts the list in descending order?
parts.ask: Say how to change the algorithm so it sorts in descending order.

points.text: Select the largest (instead of the smallest) element from list1 and move it to list2

parts.scheme: Select the largest (instead of the smallest) element from list1 and move it to list2; any valid response. Good description 2 marks.
parts.model: Change step 4 to select the largest (maximum) element from list1, and step 5 to move the largest element from list1 to list2. Then list2 fills up from the biggest value to the smallest.

steps.say: The order list2 ends up in depends on which element is picked on each pass.
Pick the largest each time instead of the smallest: change 'smallest (minimum)' to 'largest (maximum)' in steps 4 and 5.

parts.tip: Say exactly which steps change (steps 4 and 5).

parts.q: Step 4 of the algorithm says to select the smallest (minimum) element from list1. Outline a method to find the smallest element in any list.
parts.ask: Describe a step-by-step method for finding the smallest value in a list.

points.text: Initialise the minimum to be the first element in the list
Walk across the list comparing each element to the minimum so far
If the current element is less than the minimum so far, let it be the new minimum; continue to the end of the list

parts.scheme: Initialise the minimum to be the first element in the list. Then walk across the list comparing each element to the minimum so far; if the current element is less than the minimum so far, let it be the new minimum. Continue until the end of the list is reached. Pseudocode, flowchart or code also acceptable. Very good description 3 marks; fair description, or use of built-in functions, 1 mark.
parts.model: Set min to the first element of the list, then go through the rest of the list one element at a time, comparing each element with min. If the element is smaller than min, set min to that element. When the end of the list is reached, min holds the smallest element.

idea.title: Smallest so far
idea.text: You can only look at one element at a time, so keep a running 'smallest so far' and update it whenever you meet something smaller.

steps.say: Start with a guess: the first element is the smallest so far.
Visit every other element in turn and compare it with the smallest so far.
If it is smaller, it becomes the new smallest so far.
When the end of the list is reached, the smallest so far is the minimum.

parts.tip: Using Python's min() earns only 1 mark: describe the method itself.

parts.q: Step 5 of the algorithm says to move the smallest element from list1 to list2. Why would the algorithm not work if this step said to copy the smallest element from list1 to list2?
parts.ask: Explain why copying instead of moving would break the algorithm.

points.text: The same element would always be copied / list1 would remain unchanged / infinite loop
alts: unchanged|never empt|not empt|never change|not change|stays the same|remain

parts.scheme: The same element would always be copied; list1 would remain unchanged; this would result in an infinite loop. Very good explanation 2 marks.
parts.model: If the smallest element were only copied, it would stay in list1, so every pass would find the same smallest element again: list2 would fill up with copies of 14 (14, 14, 14, 14) and list1 would never change.

steps.say: Moving removes the element from list1, so the next pass finds the next smallest one.
Copying leaves it in list1, so every pass selects the same smallest element, 14, again.
list2 would end up 14, 14, 14, 14 and list1 would stay unchanged, so the list is never sorted.

parts.q: The algorithm relies on two lists to complete the sort. Describe a selection sort algorithm that would sort a list ‘in place’ i.e. without the need for a second list.
parts.ask: Describe a selection sort that works within a single list.

points.text: Pass across every element in the list from left to right (the current element)
alts: current|each position|every position|left to right|each element|every element|each index|each item|one at a time|in turn|next position|first position|move on|each time

points.text: For each current element, look for the minimum (smallest) element to its right
Swap the minimum element with the current element, then move on to the next element

parts.scheme: The algorithm passes across every element in the list (left to right); the element passed over is the current element. For each current element it looks for the minimum element to its right, which is selected and swapped with the current element; it then moves on to the next element. Pseudocode, flowchart or code also acceptable. Very good description 3 marks; fair description 1 mark.
parts.model: Start at the first position, find the smallest element from this position to the end of the list and swap it with the element in this position. Then move on to the next position and repeat, each time searching only the part to its right, until the last position is reached. The left part of the list becomes sorted without needing a second list.

idea.title: The sorted part grows from the left
idea.text: In-place selection sort treats the one list as two parts: sorted on the left, unsorted on the right. Each pass swaps the smallest unsorted value into the first unsorted position.

steps.say: Keep one list, but think of it as a sorted part (left) and an unsorted part (right); at first all of it is unsorted.
For the current position, find the smallest element from there to the end of the list.
Swap it with the element in the current position: the sorted part grows by one.
Move on to the next position and repeat until the end of the list.

parts.q:
A bookshelf is partially sorted, in alphabetic order, using the insertion sort algorithm as shown in Figure 4 below.

Fill in the empty boxes below to complete passes 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the insertion sort.
parts.ask: Write the order of the books after passes 3, 4, 5 and 6.
parts.scheme: Each correct pass 1 mark. Pass #3: B C E F A G D. Pass #4: A B C E F G D. Pass #5: A B C E F G D. Pass #6: A B C D E F G.
parts.model: Pass #3: B C E F A G D. Pass #4: A B C E F G D. Pass #5: A B C E F G D. Pass #6: A B C D E F G.

idea.title: Insertion sort
idea.text: The left part of the list is kept sorted. Each pass takes the next book from the unsorted part (the one shown in black) and slides it left into its correct place among the sorted books.

steps.say: Pass 3 inserts C: it belongs after B and before E. Result B C E F | A G D.
Pass 4 inserts A: it goes to the very front. Result A B C E F | G D.
Pass 5 inserts G: it is already after F, so nothing moves. Result A B C E F G | D.
Pass 6 inserts D between C and E. Result A B C D E F G: sorted.

parts.tip: A pass where nothing moves (pass 5) still counts: copy the row out unchanged.

parts.q: Explain how the insertion sort algorithm works.
parts.ask: Explain the steps of the insertion sort algorithm.

points.text: At the start, the first element is considered sorted and all elements to its right unsorted
It passes across each element in the list starting from the second element
On each pass the first element in the unsorted part is taken
and inserted into the sorted part at its correct position

parts.scheme: The insertion sort passes across each element in the list starting from the second element. At the start, the first element is considered sorted and all elements to its right unsorted. On each pass the first element in the unsorted list is inserted into the sorted list at its correct position. Pseudocode, flowchart or code also acceptable. Very good explanation 4 marks; good explanation 2 marks; fair 1 mark.
parts.model: Insertion sort splits the list into a sorted part, which at the start is just the first element, and an unsorted part. On each pass it takes the first element of the unsorted part (starting with the second element), compares it with the elements in the sorted part, shifting bigger ones one place to the right, and inserts it at its correct position. This repeats until the unsorted part is empty.

steps.say: At the start the first element alone counts as sorted; everything to its right is unsorted.
Each pass takes the next unsorted element, starting with the second one.
Compare it with the sorted elements to its left, shifting larger ones one place right.
Insert it in the gap at its correct position; repeat until nothing is left unsorted.

parts.tip: Describe the sorted and unsorted parts: that is what shows full understanding.

parts.q: A list that is already reversed would be considered a good test case for the insertion sort algorithm. Describe two other test cases that could be used to test the insertion sort algorithm.
parts.ask: Describe two other test lists for checking an insertion sort.

points.text: A list that is already sorted
A list where all the values are the same
A list with only two distinct values
alts: two distinct|two different|2 distinct|2 different|only two|only 2

points.text: A list where all the values are different
A list with just one element (list size 1)
alts: one element|1 element|single|one item|1 item|one value|size 1|length 1

points.text: An empty list (list size zero)
A list that is already sorted
A list where all the values are the same
A list with only two distinct values
alts: two distinct|two different|2 distinct|2 different|only two|only 2

points.text: A list where all the values are different
A list with just one element (list size 1)
alts: one element|1 element|single|one item|1 item|one value|size 1|length 1

points.text: An empty list (list size zero)

parts.scheme: For each unique test case, very good description 2 marks: a list that is already sorted; all values the same; only two distinct values; all values different; just one element (size 1); an empty list (size 0); any valid test case.
parts.model: Test case 1: a list that is already sorted, e.g. A B C D, to check that the algorithm leaves it unchanged (its best case). Test case 2: an empty list, to check that the algorithm doesn't crash when there is nothing to sort.

steps.say: Good test cases are unusual inputs that might break the algorithm (edge cases).
Already sorted: the best case; the output must be the same as the input.
Empty list or one element: there is nothing to insert, so check that it doesn't crash.
Duplicates (all values the same): check that equal values are handled correctly.

parts.tip: Give an example list for each test case and say what it checks.

parts.q: "Big O" notation is used to describe the complexity of an algorithm. Discuss the algorithmic complexity of the insertion sort algorithm using "Big O" notation.
parts.ask: Discuss insertion sort's best, average and worst cases in Big O.

points.text: Worst case is O(n²)
The worst case is a list in reverse order: for each of the n elements there are n comparisons to insert it at its correct position
Average case is also O(n²)
Best case is O(n): the list is already sorted, so there is no need to execute the inner loop

parts.scheme: Worst case is O(n²) – list in reverse order: for each of the n elements there are n comparisons required to make the insertion at the correct position; AND average case is also O(n²) / best case is O(n) – the list is already sorted so there is no need to execute the inner loop. Very good discussion 5 marks; good discussion 3 marks; fair discussion 1 mark.
parts.model: Insertion sort's worst case is O(n²), when the list is in reverse order: each of the n elements has to be compared with, and moved past, every element already sorted, about n × n steps; its average case is also O(n²). Its best case is O(n), when the list is already sorted: each element needs only one comparison and the inner loop never shifts anything. So it is slow for large unsorted lists but fast for nearly sorted ones.

idea.title: Big O
idea.text: Big O describes how the number of steps grows as the size of the input, n, grows, ignoring constants. O(n) work doubles when n doubles; O(n²) work quadruples.

steps.say: Worst case: a reversed list. Each new element is compared with every sorted element before it.
Average case: a random list needs about half as many comparisons, which is still O(n²).
Best case: an already sorted list. Each element is compared once and nothing moves.
Conclude: fine for small or nearly sorted lists, slow for large random ones.

parts.tip: Give both the best and the worst case, with the input that causes each, to reach the full 5 marks.

questions.stem:
A check digit is a single digit number used to verify numbers such as barcodes, credit cards and International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs), thereby helping to prevent data entry errors.
Check digits usually appear as the rightmost digit (position 1) of a number. For example, the check digit of the ISBN number, 1020041102 highlighted here is 2.
The general procedure used to verify ISBN numbers is as follows:
Step 1: Multiply each digit in the number by its own digit position.
Step 2: Add the 10 results together.
Step 3: Divide the total by 11.
Step 4: If the remainder is zero the ISBN number is deemed to be valid.
questions.fig: A barcode labelled ISBN 1-020041-10-2 with the check digit 2 boxed; the digits 1 0 2 0 0 4 1 1 0 2 with their digit positions 10 down to 1 written above them. Parts (b) and (c) show two Python programs.

parts.q: Apply the above procedure to verify that the ISBN number 1020041102 is valid.
parts.ask: Use the four steps to show that the ISBN 1020041102 is valid.

points.text: Step 1: each digit times its position: 10, 0, 16, 0, 0, 20, 4, 3, 0, 2
Steps 3 and 4: 55 / 11 = 5 remainder 0, so the ISBN is valid

parts.scheme: Step 1: 1x10 = 10, 0x9 = 0, 2x8 = 16, 0x7 = 0, 0x6 = 0, 4x5 = 20, 1x4 = 4, 1x3 = 3, 0x2 = 0, 2x1 = 2. Step 2: 10 + 16 + 20 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 55. Step 3: 55/11 = 5 remainder 0. Step 4: remainder = 0, so the ISBN is valid. Full correct response 3 marks; two or three correct steps 2 marks; any correct step 1 mark.

idea.title: A weighted sum
idea.text: Each digit is multiplied by a different weight (its position), so a mistyped or swapped digit changes the total and almost always stops it being a multiple of 11.

steps.say: Step 1: multiply each digit by its position, 10 for the leftmost down to 1 for the check digit.
Step 2: add the ten results.
Steps 3 and 4: divide by 11. The remainder is 0, so the ISBN is valid.

parts.tip: Show all four steps: each correct step earns marks even if you slip later.

parts.q:
Given a 9-digit number, the Python program below can be used to find the number’s check digit, that will be used as the 10th digit.
```
1    # A program to determine a check digit for a number
2    isbn = "102004110"
3    total = 0
4    for i in range(10, 1, -1):
5        total = total + int(isbn[10-i]) * i
6
7    check_digit = 11 - (total % 11)
8    print("The check digit for", isbn, "is", check_digit)
```

Line 1 of the above program contains a comment.
State two reasons why programmers use comments.

To enable the programmer to isolate a part of the code for testing
Comments used as docstrings can become part of the system documentation
Comments can contain information about the author, date, version log etc.
Make code more readable/understandable for self/others
To enable the programmer to isolate a part of the code for testing

Reason 1: explain the code so that others, or you later, can understand and maintain it.
Reason 2: record the author, date and version, or comment out lines to isolate them while testing.

A category of data that can be held in a variable / a restriction on the values that can be stored

Data type: the kind of data a value is, which decides what values it can hold and what can be done with it, e.g. isbn is a string ("102004110") while total is an integer.

steps.say: Variable: a name for a value stored in memory that can change; total is one (0, then bigger on every loop).
Data type: the kind of value it holds; isbn is a string because its value is in quotes, total is an integer.

parts.tip: Each term needs both a definition and an example from the code.

parts.q:
The program makes use of the Python int function.
Outline the purpose of the int function as it is used in the code.
parts.ask: Explain what int() does on line 5 and why it is needed.

steps.say: isbn holds a string, so isbn[10-i] gives one character, e.g. "2", not the number 2.
You can't do arithmetic with a character, so int() converts it to an integer.
Now it can be multiplied by its position i and added to total, on every pass of the loop.

parts.q: The range function on line 4 of the program generates a sequence of every integer from 10 down to 1 (but not including 1). Describe one way these integers are used in the program.
parts.ask: Describe one way the numbers from range(10, 1, -1) are used.

points.text: As a loop counter / as an index into isbn (10-i) to retrieve the next digit / as the digit position

parts.q:
The Python program below shows an alternative implementation.
```
 1  # A program to determine a check digit for a number
 2  isbn = 102004110
 3  isbn1 = isbn
 4  total = 0
 5  for i in range(2, 11):
 6      digit = isbn % 10
 7      total = total + digit*i
 8      isbn = isbn//10
 9
10  check_digit = 11 - (total % 11)
11  print("The check digit for", isbn1, "is", check_digit)
```

i = 7: isbn is 1020, so digit 0, total stays 27, isbn becomes 102.
i = 8: digit 2, total 27 + 16 = 43, isbn 10.
i = 9: digit 0, total 43, isbn 1. i = 10: digit 1, total 43 + 10 = 53, isbn 0.

questions.stem: Information systems can represent numbers in decimal, binary and hexadecimal format. Many software developers use hexadecimal numbers.

parts.q: Explain one advantage of using hexadecimal numbers.
parts.ask: Explain one advantage of using hexadecimal.

points.text: Hexadecimal is very concise: it can express numbers using fewer digits/characters than other systems
Every hex digit can be represented by a group of four binary digits, so it is easy and fast to convert between hexadecimal and binary
Because of its conciseness, humans are less likely to make mistakes writing hexadecimal (more human-friendly)
Hexadecimal is a convenient way to represent memory addresses, machine code, data, error codes, colours

parts.scheme: Hexadecimal is very concise, expressing numbers with fewer digits/characters than other number systems; every hex digit can be represented by a group of four binary digits, making conversion to and from binary easy and fast (one reason it is more human-friendly); because of its conciseness, humans are less likely to make mistakes writing it; it is a convenient way to represent memory addresses, machine code, data, error codes, colours etc. Very good description 3 marks; fair description 2 marks.
parts.model: Hexadecimal is much more compact than binary: each hex digit stands for exactly four bits, so a byte such as 11001001 can be written as just C9. Long binary values become shorter and easier for people to read and copy without mistakes, and they are still very easy to convert back to binary.

idea.title: Base 16
idea.text: Hexadecimal uses sixteen digits, 0 to 9 then A to F (A = 10, …, F = 15). Since 16 = 2⁴, one hex digit always equals one group of 4 bits (a nibble).

steps.say: Compare lengths: the byte 11001001 takes 8 binary digits but only 2 hex digits.
Say why it works: 16 = 2⁴, so each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, which makes converting to binary quick.
State the advantage: shorter, more human-friendly and fewer mistakes when writing values such as memory addresses or colours.

parts.tip: Say why it is an advantage (e.g. fewer mistakes), not just 'it is shorter'.

parts.q: Convert the hexadecimal number C9 into a decimal number.

questions.topic: Wolf, goat and cabbage: representing states
questions.stem:
A farmer needs to ferry a wolf, a goat and a cabbage from one side of a river to the other in a boat, as shown in Figure 3. However, the boat only has room for the farmer and one other item, either the wolf, the goat or the cabbage. If left alone without the farmer present, the wolf would eat the goat, and the goat would eat the cabbage.
The state of the system at any given point in time can be represented using an ordered list of four values as follows:
(<side for farmer>, <side for wolf>, <side for goat>, <side for cabbage>)
By using the letter E to represent the east side of the river, and the letter W to represent the west side of the river, the state (E, E, E, E) means that all four are on the east side of the river.
(E, E, E, E) is the initial state of the system.
questions.fig: Figure 3: cartoon of a wolf, a goat and a cabbage on a river bank, with the farmer in a small boat.

parts.q: Using this notation, what is the desired final state of the system?
parts.ask: Write the final state in the (farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage) notation.
parts.scheme: (W, W, W, W). Correct response 1 mark.
parts.model: (W, W, W, W)

idea.title: A state is an abstraction
idea.text: The whole puzzle is reduced to four letters, one for each of the farmer, wolf, goat and cabbage, saying which bank it is on. Everything else (the boat, the river, the time) is left out.

steps.say: The goal is to get the farmer and all three items across to the other side, the west bank.
So every one of the four positions is W: (W, W, W, W).

parts.q:
The state (W, E, E, W) is considered a loss state because the wolf will eat the goat (as the farmer and the cabbage are both on the west side).
Using this notation, name any other two loss states.
parts.ask: Write two other states in which something gets eaten.
parts.scheme: 2 marks each for two of: (E, E, W, W), (E, W, W, E), (E, W, W, W), (W, E, E, E), (W, W, E, E). (W, E, E, W) earns no marks as it is given in the question.
parts.model: 1. (W, W, E, E): the farmer and wolf are on the west side, so the goat eats the cabbage on the east side. 2. (E, E, W, W): the goat and cabbage are alone on the west side, so the goat eats the cabbage.

steps.say: Something gets eaten when the goat is on the opposite side from the farmer and shares that side with the wolf or the cabbage.
Farmer W, goat and cabbage left on E: (W, W, E, E). The goat eats the cabbage.
Farmer E, goat on W with the cabbage: (E, E, W, W). The goat eats the cabbage.
Other loss states work the same way, e.g. (E, W, W, E): the wolf eats the goat on the west side.

parts.tip: Check each state: is the goat away from the farmer and with the wolf or the cabbage?

parts.q: Using this notation, name any one non-loss state, other than the initial and final states.
parts.ask: Write one safe state that is not the start or the end.
parts.scheme: 1 mark for any of: (E, E, E, W), (E, E, W, E), (E, W, E, E), (E, W, E, W), (W, E, W, E), (W, E, W, W), (W, W, E, W), (W, W, W, E).
parts.model: (W, E, W, E): the farmer has taken the goat across, and the wolf and the cabbage are safe together on the east side.

steps.say: A state is safe if the goat is with the farmer, or the goat is on a side with neither the wolf nor the cabbage.
For example, (W, E, W, E): the farmer and the goat are on the west side; the wolf won't eat the cabbage.

questions.stem:
Chop Cup is a magic routine which involves three cups face down and one ball underneath one of the cups. In any single move the position of two cups can be swapped using one of three possible moves, A, B or C as shown in Figure 4 below.
Each cup is identified by its position. Initially the leftmost cup is at position 1, the middle cup is at position 2 and the right cup is at position 3.
questions.fig: Figure 4: three cups in a row. Move A swaps the cups in positions 1 and 2; Move B swaps positions 1 and 3; Move C swaps positions 2 and 3.

parts.q: Given that the ball starts under the leftmost cup (position 1) and always remains under the same cup, state the ball position after the sequence of moves, ABCBCA.
parts.ask: Follow the ball through the moves ABCBCA and give its final position.
parts.scheme: Ball position after each move: A 2, B 2, C 3, B 1, C 1, A 2. Answer: the ball position after ABCBCA is 2 (under the middle cup). Correct 4 marks; half correct 2 marks; response with some merit 1 mark.
parts.model: 2 (the ball ends under the middle cup).

idea.title: Follow one thing
idea.text: You don't need to track all three cups: only follow the ball. A move changes the ball's position only if it swaps the cup the ball is under.

steps.say: Write down what each move swaps: A swaps 1 and 2, B swaps 1 and 3, C swaps 2 and 3.
Start at 1. A (1↔2) moves it to 2. B (1↔3) doesn't touch 2. C (2↔3) moves it to 3.
B (1↔3) moves it to 1. C (2↔3) doesn't touch 1. A (1↔2) moves it to 2.
The ball finishes at position 2, under the middle cup.

parts.tip: Write the position after every move, so a slip still earns part of the marks.

parts.q: Without knowing which cup the ball is under, construct a sequence involving at least three moves which results in the ball ending in the same position as it started from.
parts.ask: Type a sequence of at least 3 moves, as letters, that returns the ball.
parts.scheme: Any correct sequence, 2 marks: any 'same move' an even number of times (at least 4), e.g. AAAA, BBBBBB; any even-length palindromic sequence, e.g. ABBA, ABCCBA; any other correct sequence (the four-move ones are AAAA, AABB, AACC, ABAC, ABBA, ABCB, ACAB, ACBC, ACCA, BAAB, BABC, BACA, BBAA, BBBB, BBCC, BCAC, BCBA, BCCB, CAAC, CABA, CACB, CBAB, CBBC, CBCA, CCAA, CCBB, CCCC). Odd-length sequences will not work.
parts.model: ABBA

idea.title: Every swap undoes itself
idea.text: Doing the same swap twice puts the cups back. So any sequence followed by the same moves in reverse order, a palindrome like ABBA, returns every cup to where it started.

steps.say: The ball could be under any cup, so every cup must end where it started.
Each swap undoes itself: AA leaves everything unchanged.
So undo your moves in reverse order: AB followed by BA gives ABBA, and every cup is back in place.
Three moves can't work: an odd number of swaps always leaves two cups swapped, so you need at least four.

parts.tip: Check your sequence with the ball starting at each of positions 1, 2 and 3.

questions.stem: Quicksort is widely recognised as one of the most efficient sorting algorithms. It works by recursively partitioning a list about one of the elements known as the pivot. Consider the unsorted list of integers shown in Figure 5 below and answer the questions that follow.

parts.q: Using the leftmost element as the pivot, show the contents of the list after the initial partition by the quicksort algorithm. You should assume that the elements in the left and right sub-lists are not re-ordered.
parts.ask: Write the list after the first partition about the leftmost element.
parts.scheme: 30 40 10 50 20 60 80 70 90 (or 50 30 20 40 10 60 80 70 90). Elements split about the pivot 1 mark; left sub-list correct 1 mark; right sub-list correct 1 mark.

idea.title: Partitioning
idea.text: Partitioning puts the pivot in its final sorted place, with every smaller element to its left and every larger one to its right. Quicksort then sorts each side in the same way.

steps.say: The pivot is the leftmost element: 60.
Pick out the elements smaller than 60, keeping their order: 30, 40, 10, 50, 20.
Pick out the elements bigger than 60, keeping their order: 80, 70, 90.
Write the left sub-list, then the pivot, then the right sub-list.

parts.q: Explain why 90 would have been a poor choice of pivot to partition the list shown in Figure 5.
parts.ask: Explain why 90 would be a bad pivot for this list.

points.text: Because 90 is the largest number in the list
so all the other elements end up on one side, which increases the time taken to execute the algorithm

parts.scheme: Because 90 is the largest number in the list; because it would increase the time taken to execute the algorithm. Very good description 3 marks; fair description 2 marks.
parts.model: 90 is the largest number in the list, so partitioning around it puts all eight other numbers in the left sub-list and nothing in the right. The list is hardly split at all, so quicksort needs many more partitions and takes much longer to run.

steps.say: A good pivot splits the list into two parts of similar size.
90 is the largest value, so every other element goes to its left and the right sub-list is empty.
The problem has only shrunk by one element, so many more partitions are needed: the sort is slower.

questions.topic: Digital hubs: routes, abstraction and heuristics
questions.stem: The National Hub Network is an initiative set up by the Irish Government to allow people across Ireland to work closer to home through providing digital working hubs with modern facilities and high-speed internet connections. parts.q: Consider the impact that a digital working hub might have to a rural community’s culture and society. Provide one argument in support of this initiative and one argument against.
parts.ask: Give one argument for and one against digital hubs in rural areas.

points.text: Local community and businesses can avail of dependable IT facilities/online services
Residents who had to work in towns/cities can now work in their local area instead of leaving
Facilities might attract new people to live in the area
Boost to the local economy
House prices could increase due to high earners
Possible negative impact on local culture, community and way of life
Increased population could drain the infrastructure and resources in place
New businesses coming to the area could impact other businesses

questions.stem: Computers can use a choice of different search algorithms to find information much quicker than humans. Two common search algorithms are the linear search and the binary search.

parts.q:
The Python code below shows an implementation of a binary search function.
```
 1  def binary_search1(v, L):
 2
 3      lo = 0
 4      hi = len(L) - 1
 5
 6      while (lo <= hi):
 7          mid = (lo + hi)//2
 8
 9          if L[mid] > v:
10              hi = mid - 1
11          elif L[mid] < v:
12              lo = mid + 1
13          else:
14              return mid
15
16      return len(L)
```

In the code there is one example of iteration. State on which lines the iteration starts and ends and explain what it does.
parts.ask: Give the lines where the loop starts and ends and explain what it does.

points.text: The loop repeatedly calculates the middle index and compares the value there with the target value
and updates the lower and higher indices until the value is found or the search range becomes empty (lo crosses over hi)

parts.scheme: Start line number 6 (1 mark); end line number 14 (1 mark). Explanation (very good 3 marks, fair 2): the loop repeatedly divides the list in half by calculating the middle index, compares the value at the middle index with the target value, and updates the lower and higher indices accordingly until the target value is found or the search range becomes empty (the lower index crossing over the higher index).
parts.model: Start line number: 6. End line number: 14. Explain: the while loop repeatedly works out the middle position of the part of the list still being searched and compares the value there with v. If the middle value is too big it moves hi down to mid - 1, if too small it moves lo up to mid + 1, halving the search range each time, until v is found (and returned) or lo passes hi, which means v is not in the list.

steps.say: Iteration means a loop: here it is the while loop that starts on line 6.
Its body is the indented block, which ends with return mid on line 14.
Each pass finds the middle, compares it with v and moves lo or hi to keep only the half that could hold v.
It stops when v is found or lo > hi (nothing left to search).

parts.scheme: It is used to indicate that the value has not been found. Very good explanation 3 marks; fair explanation 2 marks.
parts.model: If the loop ends without finding v, the function returns len(L). That number is one past the last valid index (the indexes go from 0 to len(L) - 1), so it can never be a real position: it tells the calling code that the value was not found.

steps.say: Line 16 is only reached if the loop finishes without returning, so v was not found.
len(L) is one more than the last index, so it can't be confused with a real position: it signals 'not found'.

parts.q:
An alternative implementation of the binary search can be achieved using recursion as shown.
```
 1  def binary_search2(v, L, lo, hi):
 2
 3      if lo > hi:
 4          return len(L)
 5
 6      mid = (lo + hi)//2
 7
 8      if L[mid] > v:
 9          return binary_search2(v, L, lo, mid-1)
10      elif L[mid] < v:
11          return binary_search2(v, L, mid+1, hi)
12
13      return mid
```

Referring to the code above, describe two properties of recursive functions.
parts.ask: Describe two properties of recursive functions, using the code.

points.text: A recursive function must call itself (lines 9 and 11)
A recursive function must have a base case/exit criteria which ends the recursion (lo > hi, line 3)
Progressive approach: it must move towards its base case (mid-1 and mid+1 reset lo and hi, lines 9 and 11)
A recursive function must call itself (lines 9 and 11)
A recursive function must have a base case/exit criteria which ends the recursion (lo > hi, line 3)
Progressive approach: it must move towards its base case (mid-1 and mid+1 reset lo and hi, lines 9 and 11)

parts.scheme: A recursive function must call itself (lines 9 and 11; each call's context goes on the call stack); it must have a base case/exit criteria that ends the recursion, the smallest problem solved directly (lo > hi, line 3); it must move towards its base case (mid-1 and mid+1 reset lo and hi in each call, lines 9 and 11). For each property: very good 3 marks, fair 2 marks.
parts.model: Property 1: a recursive function calls itself: binary_search2 calls binary_search2 on lines 9 and 11, each time on half of the list. Property 2: it must have a base case that stops the recursion: on line 3, if lo > hi there is nothing left to search and it returns len(L) without calling itself again.

steps.say: Look for where the function calls itself: lines 9 and 11.
Look for where it stops calling itself: the base case lo > hi on line 3.
Each call uses mid-1 or mid+1, so the range shrinks and it always reaches the base case.

parts.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using recursion.
parts.ask: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of recursion.

points.text: Simplicity, elegance and conciseness
More readable and efficient algorithm descriptions
Lends itself to breaking problems down into smaller similar problems
Performance: slower execution due to memory overheads
If the recursion is too deep it can run out of stack space and the program crashes

parts.scheme: Advantages: simplicity, elegance and conciseness; more readable and efficient algorithm descriptions; lends itself to breaking problems down into smaller similar problems. Disadvantages: performance, slower execution due to memory overheads; if recursion is too deep the stack can run out of space and the program crashes. For each: very good 3 marks, fair 2 marks.
parts.model: Advantage: recursion breaks a problem into smaller versions of the same problem, so the code can be short and elegant, like binary_search2. Disadvantage: every call takes up memory on the call stack, so recursion is slower and, if it goes too deep, the stack runs out of space and the program crashes.

steps.say: Advantage: short, elegant code that mirrors how the problem splits into smaller copies of itself.
Disadvantage: each call uses memory on the stack, which is slower and can overflow if the recursion is too deep.
